pages.text: Jordan church shooting leaves seven dead, officials say Skip to content Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Weather Newsletters Watch Live Seven shot dead by gunmen at church funeral in Jordan, officials say 23 October 2026 Share Save Add as preferred on Google Jamie Whitehead and Jacob Phillips Watch: CCTV footage appears to show gunmen near church Seven people have been killed in an attack on a funeral in central Jordan, officials have said. At least 34 others were injured as gunmen opened fire on a church in Hmoud, in the Karak governorate on Friday. The unidentified gunmen are reported to have arrived in a car, entered the church and opened fire before fleeing. No-one has admitted carrying out the attack. In a news conference, Interior Minister Mazen al-Faraya said authorities were working to apprehend the perpetrators which he described as a "group of extremists". Jordan's King Abdullah II said authorities would "confront the terrorist act that targeted Karak with the harshest penalties". Initial reports indicated seven people had been killed in the attack. A government spokesperson later said six people had died, before officials again revised the death toll to seven. CCTV footage, verified by the BBC, appears to show three gunmen making their way from a road toward the church. Two of the attackers are seen making their way on to what appears to be a vehicle entrance to the church grounds, before retreating briefly and returning with a third man. pages.description: People know Josh Kerr the athlete. But are there two Josh Kerrs? The mile world record holder talks about disguising alcohol-free cider, entering races under a false name and his granny keeping him humble.
pages.text: Josh Kerr: The Making of the Man Behind the Shades - BBC Sport By Richard Winton BBC Sport Scotland You know Josh Kerr, right? The guy with the shades. The fastest man to ever run a mile. Scottish, but with a curious transatlantic accent. Slicked-back hair. Beard. Usually got a medal of some kind slung around his neck. No stranger to telling you what he thinks. That's Kerr the competitor, one of the foremost faces in world athletics, and a man who rampaged around London's Olympic Stadium in three minutes 42.66 seconds in July to set a new world record - then followed it up with a home Commonwealth gold and an imperious triumph at the Ultimate Championship. Kerr recognises the description, smiling as it's articulated. But is there another version of him? Speaking to him during one of his regular returns to Scotland from his New Mexico base, it becomes clear there is. There's scant chat about records, medals and his enjoyably niggly rivalry with Jakob Ingebrigtsen. Instead, he talks about disguising alcohol-free cider, entering races under a false name, cold-calling universities, being starstruck meeting Scotland's rugby players and his granny keeping him humble. This is the Kerr who spent the thick end of an hour on a chilly August evening taking selfies, signing his name and sharing his wisdom with young fans at Scotstoun after his Commonwealth medal presentation. The Kerr who is still a regular visitor to first club Edinburgh AC's training sessions. This is Uncle Josh, who is heading for a party with his nephews after this chat. pages.description: The animals that plummeted 85 feet into Wyoming’s Natural Trap Cave provide a layered history of life dating back to the Pleistocene
pages.text: Journey Into a Prehistoric Cave That Trapped and Entombed Animals for Millennia Skip to main content Illustration by Emily Lankiewicz / Photos courtesy of Dr. Susumu Tomiya and public domain Natural Trap Cave is a pit in northern Wyoming into which countless animals have fallen and met their untimely demise since the Pleistocene. Paleontologists today find the cave a treasure trove — a stunning record of the species that have long roamed the area. The mammalian fossils left behind shed light on the climate, food sources and migration patterns of these species from earlier eras. Careful excavation work over the years that has involved sifting for bones, extracting ancient DNA, and looking for prehistoric pollen has revealed not just the plants and animals that once populated this part of the world, but also the ecosystems and climates that governed it. It also has required some rather advanced rappelling skills. In this episode, host Ari Daniel speaks with vertebrate paleontologist Julie Meachen and Smithsonian contributing writer Michael Ray Taylor about what rappelling into Natural Trap Cave reveals about its contents and what it can tell us about Earth’s past. L’ONU célèbre chaque année six « Journées de la langue », consacrées aux six langues officielles des Nations Unies, qui sont l’arabe, le chinois, l’anglais, le français, le russe et l’espagnol. La date de la Journée de la langue française a été choisie symboliquement en référence au 20 mars 1970, qui marque la création de l'Agence de coopération culturelle et technique (ACCT), devenue l’ Organisation internationale de la Francophonie (OIF) . Facteur essentiel d’une communication harmonieuse entre les peuples, le multilinguisme revêt plus que jamais une importance toute particulière pour l’ONU car il favorise la tolérance et assure la participation effective de tous

pages.text: JPR Williams: a revolutionary, a fighter and the ultimate competitor | Wales rugby union team | The Guardian Skip to main content Skip to navigation JPR Williams: a rugby union great who changed full-back role – video obituary Wales rugby union team This article is more than 2 years old JPR Williams: a revolutionary, a fighter and the ultimate competitor This article is more than 2 years old Paul Rees The foresight of a primary school teacher in Wales helped to create one of the best attacking full-backs of the 1970s Tue 9 Jan 2024 12.28 EST Last modified on Wed 10 Jan 2024 05.27 EST Share J PR Williams described himself as a diehard Corinthian, but he was also a revolutionary. When he made his debut for Wales against Scotland in 1969, it was in a position then regarded as the last line of defence. Only 15 tries had been scored by full-backs in major Test matches in 88 years, but the former British junior tennis champion changed the dynamic and smoothed the way for players such as Andy Irvine, Serge Blanco and John Gallagher. Williams, who qualified as an orthopaedic surgeon while playing for London Welsh, scored six tries in his 55 internationals for Wales, five against England, an opponent he boasted a 100% success rate against in 11 Tests. He was qualified to wear the white jersey as his mother, Margaret, was born in Rochdale, but there was never the remotest chance of a boy born and raised in the Bridgend area turning his back on his homeland. pages.text: Jurassic period information and facts | National Geographic SCIENCE What is the Jurassic period and why did it end? The heyday of dinosaurs, the Jurassic era saw Earth’s climate change from hot and dry to humid and subtropical. The Jurassic period was characterized by a warm, wet climate that gave rise to lush vegetation and abundant life. Many new dinosaurs emerged—in great numbers. Above, Dimorphodon reptiles fly over a herd of Mamenchisaurus dinosaurs coming down to a river for a drink. Illustration by CoreyFord, Getty Images By National Geographic Staff Last updated August 18, 2025 The Jurassic is a geologic period that took place about 201.3 million years to 145 million years ago and constitutes the middle part of the Mesozoic era . The Jurassic period was named after the Jura limestone deposits in the Jura Mountains, discovered by German geologist Alexander von Humboldt . Building on this find, French scientist Alexandre Brongniart later coined the Jurassic period. There are three Jurassic time periods: early, middle, and late. Overall, the Jurassic gives us a particularly well-preserved fossil record of prehistoric life, which included theropod dinosaurs that scientists believe evolved to become birds . Thanks to this rich record, we know that the Jurassic was the age of dinosaurs roaming a tropical Earth filled with ferns, flowering plants, and conifers. It was also a time when sea monsters, sharks, and blood-red plankton filled inland seas borne of crumbling landmasses. Here’s what the Jurassic period was really like. pages.text: Justice Outcomes Explorer (JOE) Justice Outcomes Explorer (JOE) Skip Navigation Justice Outcomes Explorer (JOE) May 01, 2024 The Justice Outcomes Explorer (JOE) is a Census Bureau experimental data product that measures the economic and health outcomes of people who have been involved with the criminal justice system. Criminal justice involvement can include criminal charges, prison releases, and probation and parole sentences. Outcomes measured include employment, earnings, government program participation, and mortality. JOE is a collaboration between the U.S. Census Bureau and the University of Michigan that uses Criminal Justice Administrative Records System (CJARS) data to better understand how people involved in the justice system reintegrate into society. JOE covers criminal justice system involvement at any point between 2000 and 2020. Actual coverage of justice involvement depends on the coverage of agencies in the CJARS data, while coverage of outcomes depends on the availability of source data at the Census Bureau. Data users can download JOE data below or interact directly with the JOE data using the data visualization tool hosted by the University of Michigan. The tool includes additional justice-related outcomes created from CJARS without Census Bureau data. Justin Bis Justin Bis is the Chief of Staff for the Office of Technology Commercialization (OTC) at the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE). In this role, he works alongside OTC leadership to maximize the impact of DOE’s investments in technology commercialization, strengthen coordination across the agency, and ensure long-term success. Mr. Bis has more than a decade of experience in government service and public life. He previously served at the White House as Special Assistant to President Trump and Deputy Director of the Presidential Personnel Office, where he managed the appointment of senior government officials responsible for regulating the U.S. financial and energy markets. At DOE, he was the Director of Intergovernmental and External Affairs under Secretary Dan Brouillette, serving as the department’s primary liaison to trade associations, labor unions, and state, local, and tribal governments. Beyond his federal service, Mr. Bis was the Executive Director of the Ohio Republican Party and Ohio Deputy State Director for the Donald J. Trump for President campaign. He holds a Bachelor of Arts in Political Science from Northern Michigan University.

Juston Fontaine Juston Fontaine is the Deputy Director for Operations in the Department of Energy’s Office of Science. In this capacity, Mr. Fontaine is responsible for management and operational oversight of the Office of Science complex, including 10 national laboratories executing leading scientific research and development. In addition to his position as Deputy Director, Mr. Fontaine also serves as the Office of Science Head of Contracting Activity. Mr. Fontaine has over 20 years of experience with the Department of Energy, serving in a variety of roles to provide leadership and coordination on a wide range of complex operational and technical issues, as well as oversight of agency programs and operations. Prior to joining the Office of Science, Mr. Fontaine was the Chief of Staff for the Office of the Under Secretary for Management and Performance. In this capacity, he led day-to-day operations of the Office of the Under Secretary, coordinating project management and the mission support functions of the Department. Photograph: Courtesy of Hybe K-pop K-pop group NewJeans’s contract omitted rights to ‘sleep and free choice’ – report New report finds that record label Ador stripped child protections from group’s contracts when they were minors Owen Myers Thu 5 Nov 2026 12.08 EST Last modified on Thu 5 Nov 2026 16.56 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The superstar K-pop group NewJeans signed restrictive record label contracts that waived their right to “sleep, rest and free choice”. A new report from the New York Times found that the contracts were signed when the members of the record-breaking girl group were aged 14 to 17. NewJeans member Danielle sued for millions after bitter feud with K-pop record label Read more The contracts banned the performers from having an “insincere attitude” and engaging in “inappropriate romantic relationships”. They also struck standard child protection language which protected “basic human rights” including the group members’ right to education. The contracts from record label Ador (a subsidiary of Hybe, home of the popular groups BTS and Katseye ) additionally excluded portions of the Korean government’s K-pop contract template stipulating that the label “shall not demand that a performer who is a minor engage in excessive physical exposure or overly sexually suggestive expression”. There are more miles of singletrack, more places to camp and dedicated space for races and other large events, all part of a broader effort by the Bureau of Land Management and community partners to keep pace with one of western Colorado’s busiest recreation areas. This fall, the final trail in the North Fruita Desert Trails Master Plan is complete. K2-Play winds for about three miles along the base of the Book Cliffs and completes the final phase of a roughly 30-mile expansion of the 18 Road trail system. Its completion caps years of planning and construction involving the BLM Grand Junction Field Office, Colorado Plateau Mountain Bike Trail Association, Mesa County, City of Fruita, local businesses, professional trail builders and volunteers. pages.description: Usman Khawaja's autobiography has exposed the limbo Australian cricket finds itself stuck in over the sandpaper scandal, writes Stephan Shemilt.
pages.text: Khawaja book: Sandpapergate a stench Cricket Australia cannot shake - BBC Sport Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Pat Cummins has led Australia in 43 Tests since 2021 By Stephan Shemilt Cricket Correspondent Published 10 November 2026 There are stories that can damage reputations, tarnish legacies and put asterisks next to achievements. Never-ending sagas, claim and counterclaim, one word against another. Are Pep Guardiola's trophies at Manchester City rendered worthless by financial rule breaches? Would either of the Houston Astros or Boston Red Sox have won the World Series without sign stealing? How much fake blood was spilled by Harlequins? Now, sandpapergate has morphed into Usman Khawaja's-book-gate, opening old wounds and asking questions that have hung over Australian cricket since Cameron Bancroft hid some DIY equipment in his jockstrap in 2018. Published on Tuesday, Khawaja's autobiography – Sabr – is only suggesting what plenty have suspected for the past eight years. It always seemed likely that Bancroft, Steve Smith and David Warner were not the only three members of the Australia camp with knowledge of the sandpaper plot. Careful with his words, perhaps for legal reasons, Khawaja has said enough to reignite a row that once consumed the entire nation of Australia. Crucially, the former batter has not named individuals and, in the opinion of Cricket Australia (CA), not presented enough evidence to merit a new investigation. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites. https://www.nist.gov/si-redefinition/kilogram/kilogram-kibble-balance SI Redefinition Kilogram: The Kibble Balance Named after its inventor, Bryan Kibble at the U.K.’s National Physical Laboratory (NPL) , who conceptualized it in 1975, the Kibble balance is an exquisitely accurate weighing machine. Like any balance, it is designed to equalize one force with another: In this case, the weight of a test mass is exactly offset by a force produced when an electrical current is run through a coil of wire immersed in a surrounding magnetic field. The surrounding field is provided by a large permanent magnet system or an electromagnet. The moveable coil, once electrified, becomes an electromagnet with a field strength proportional to the amount of current it conducts. When the coil's field interacts with the surrounding magnetic field, an upward force is exerted on the coil. The magnitude of that force is controlled by adjusting the current. Basic principles of the Kibble balance, a device that can be used to measure mass. pages.text: Kim Ng talks AUSL future, MLB career on podcast Skip to Content Before trailblazer Kim Ng had a resume brimming with unprecedented achievements – including becoming the first woman hired as general manager for a major North American men’s sports team – she was a Yankees fan playing stickball in the streets of Queens with her father, using cars and manholes to signify bases. Growing up, her favorite Yankees were Thurman Munson and Lou Piniella, while her women’s sports heroes included tennis players Billie Jean King and Martina Navratilova. When it came to bat and ball sports, there weren’t exactly women stars for her to look up to. Now, two years into Ng’s tenure at the helm of the Athletes Unlimted Softball League , young girls don’t just have professional players they can see themselves in: they have a commissioner, too. pages.text: Kimi Antonelli - the boy 'born in a garage' and made on the track - BBC Sport By Andrew Benson F1 Correspondent This is an updated version of an article first published in August 2026 Kimi Antonelli was 10 when his father Marco first realised the boy sitting on his lap, operating the steering and gears, might have an exceptional talent as a racing driver. The pair were at the Adria circuit in north-east Italy, Marco with his Lamborghini sports car team, Kimi competing in a karting race. It was the end of the day and Marco, a former driver himself, asked his son: "Do you want to try the Lamborghini?" Of course he did. Marco strapped himself and Kimi into the car, belts extended around both. Dad was in charge of the throttle and brake, his son would control the rest. "I couldn't see the track because he was in front of me with a helmet on," Marco tells BBC Sport. "I could only see beside me the marker panels before each corner - 100m, 50m. "We started to drive, step by step, faster, faster, faster. In the end, I pushed like I was alone and I arrived at the braking point at the end of the straight, 320km/h, braked very hard and at the limit. "The car had a lot of oversteer. Kimi controlled the oversteer perfectly, then I went on the throttle, Kimi finished the oversteer, changed gear, and went. "I said: 'OK, stop, because it has now become dangerous.' But when I saw the video, 10 years old, on my leg, oversteer, everything perfect, I said: 'Maybe he has something special.'"
